name: Common Gingerbread
description: Historical recipe from Miss Leslie's Complete Cookery (1851). Source method; not modernized or kitchen-tested.

ingredients.name: West India molasses
ingredients.originalText: a quart of West India molasses

ingredients.name: brown sugar
ingredients.originalText: half a pound of brown sugar

ingredients.name: large tea-spoonful of powdered cloves
ingredients.originalText: a large tea-spoonful of powdered cloves

instructions.text: Cut up a pound of butter in a quart of West India molasses, which must be perfectly sweet
Warm it slightly, just enough to melt the butter
Crush with the rolling-pin, on the paste-board, half a pound of brown sugar
Add it by degrees to the molasses and butter
Stir in three table-spoonfuls of ginger, a large tea-spoonful of powdered cloves, and a tea-spoonful of powdered cinnamon
Add gradually sufficient flour to make a dough stiff enough to roll out easily
Add a small tea-spoonful of pearl-ash melted in a little sour milk
Mix and stir the dough very hard with a spaddle, or a wooden spoon, but do not knead it
Divide it with a knife into equal portions
Having floured your hands, roll it out on the paste-board into long even strips
Place them in shallow tin pans, that have been buttered, either laying the strips side by side in straight round sticks, or coil them into rings one within another
Bake them in a brisk oven, taking care that they do not burn

source.author: Eliza Leslie
source.originalInstructions:
1. Cut up a pound of butter in a quart of West India molasses, which must be perfectly sweet
2. Warm it slightly, just enough to melt the butter
3. Crush with the rolling-pin, on the paste-board, half a pound of brown sugar
4. Add it by degrees to the molasses and butter
5. Stir in three table-spoonfuls of ginger, a large tea-spoonful of powdered cloves, and a tea-spoonful of powdered cinnamon
6. Add gradually sufficient flour to make a dough stiff enough to roll out easily
7. Add a small tea-spoonful of pearl-ash melted in a little sour milk
8. Mix and stir the dough very hard with a spaddle, or a wooden spoon, but do not knead it
9. Divide it with a knife into equal portions
10. Having floured your hands, roll it out on the paste-board into long even strips
11. Place them in shallow tin pans, that have been buttered, either laying the strips side by side in straight round sticks, or coil them into rings one within another
12. Bake them in a brisk oven, taking care that they do not burn
